638.title: Grace after meals
638.hook: four blessings: for food, for the land, for Jerusalem, for goodness
638.howItsDone: After a meal with bread, observant Jews recite Birkat HaMazon, usually from a small booklet called a bencher; on Shabbat and holidays it is often sung together at the table, with extra passages for the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses' five words for Miriam. Your line was both are real prayer. Today, a prayer that isn't short at all, and comes when most people are reaching for their coats.

In a lot of homes, grace comes first. The food is hot, everyone's hungry, someone says a few words, and the forks come out. Jewish tradition does have a blessing before the meal: the short one over bread, thanking God who brings forth bread from the earth. But the big one, the one the Torah actually commands, comes after. When the plates are empty and you're full and a little sleepy and nobody needs anything. That's exactly the moment the Torah picks.
screen: `GRACE BEFORE THE FORKS.` → `A SHORT BLESSING OVER BREAD.` → `THE BIG ONE COMES AFTER.`

segments.voice: The source is in Deuteronomy: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee." Eat, be satisfied, bless. In that order. The rabbis read this as the command for Birkat HaMazon, the blessing for food. Its core is four blessings, and the Talmud, in Berakhot 48b, tells a story about where each came from. The first, for food, thanks God who feeds the whole world. The tradition says Moses composed it when the manna began to fall in the desert. The second, for the land, thanks God for the good land, and for the covenant and the Torah. Tradition credits Joshua, when the people entered the land. The third asks for mercy on Jerusalem and its rebuilding; it's linked to David and Solomon, who made the city a capital and built the Temple. The fourth is later, and its story is sad. After the Romans crushed the revolt at Betar, the dead lay unburied for a long time. When permission to bury them finally came, the sages at Yavneh added a blessing: to the One who is good and does good. Good, that the bodies had not decayed. Good, that they could finally be buried. A blessing for goodness, born in grief. Together they trace a whole history, from the desert to the land to the city to the ruins and back to gratitude. Many Jews sing it, especially on Shabbat, and it can take several minutes. A full stomach turns into a short history lesson in thanks.

segments.voice: Think back to the last thing you ate and walk the four blessings in your own way: the food and whoever grew and cooked it, the ground it came from, a place you love and want to see whole, and one good thing in your life, even if it came out of something hard. If you pray, you can say the thanks to God.
Birkat HaMazon. The blessing for food: four blessings, for food, the land, Jerusalem and goodness, said when you're already full.
Your line: four thanks after eating. Eat, be satisfied, bless, in that order. See you tomorrow.

639.title: Three at the table
639.hook: when three eat together, one invites the others to bless
639.howItsDone: When three or more Jewish adults eat bread together, one leads the zimmun, the invitation to grace, and the others respond before Birkat HaMazon; with ten, the word Eloheinu is added. Who may lead and join varies between communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Birkat HaMazon, grace after meals. Your line was four thanks after eating. Today, what changes when you're not eating alone.

Friday night. The meal is over, plates pushed back, someone still picking at the cake. Then one person clears their throat and says, half singing, in Yiddish or Hebrew: friends, let's bless. Everyone stops and answers. It's a tiny call and response, maybe fifteen seconds long, and it only happens when at least three people ate together. Two people bless on their own. Three become something else.
screen: `THE PLATES PUSHED BACK.` → `FRIENDS, LET'S BLESS.` → `ONLY WHEN THERE ARE THREE.`

segments.voice: It's called zimmun, an invitation, from a root that means to call together. The Mishnah in Berakhot rules that three who ate together are obligated to make it. The Talmud finds the source in a psalm: "O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt His name together." One person invites, the others join. In many homes it goes like this. The leader says: friends, let us bless, in Hebrew rabbotai nevarech, or in the old Yiddish, rabbosai, mir vellen bentshen. Everyone answers with a verse from Psalm 113: "Blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and for ever." The leader repeats it, then says: let us bless the One whose food we have eaten. The table answers: blessed is the One whose food we have eaten, and through whose goodness we live. Then the grace continues. With ten people, God's name, Eloheinu, our God, is added to the invitation. The Talmud also says that women may form a zimmun of their own. In some communities today, men and women together, or women leading, are welcomed; in others, practice stays more traditional. Each community follows its own teachers. What's striking is the shape. Someone has to ask the others to join, and they have to say yes out loud. A meal shared becomes thanks shared, and for a minute the table turns into a small congregation.

segments.voice: Picture the next meal you'll share with at least two other people and the moment it ends: imagine being the one who says, before we get up, let's say thank you, and hearing them answer. If you pray, you can picture the zimmun itself, or the psalm's let us exalt His name together; if not, a simple let's thank whoever made this will do. Then sit for a while with who's at that table.

640.title: Any language (Mishnah Sotah 7:1)
640.hook: the Shema, Amidah and grace may be said in any language one understands
640.tomorrow: Siddur close: prayer shapes the day
640.howItsDone: Many Jewish communities pray mainly in Hebrew, with translations printed beside the text; Reform and some other communities include substantial prayer in the local language, and many individuals add personal prayers in their mother tongue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the zimmun: three at the table, and one invites the rest. Your line was let us bless. Today, which language the blessing has to be in.

Saturday morning, three synagogues, three cities, Hebrew in each of them. But listen closer. In one, the rabbi reads a prayer in English. In another, an old man murmurs a translation in Russian under his breath. In a third, the children sing a line in Spanish. Some people assume Jewish prayer only counts in Hebrew. The Mishnah took up that question long before anyone printed a translated prayer book, and its answer was a list.
screen: `HEBREW IN EACH OF THEM.` → `ENGLISH, RUSSIAN, SPANISH.` → `DOES IT COUNT?`

segments.voice: In tractate Sotah, the Mishnah lists things that may be said in any language. Among them: the Shema, the tefillah, which means the Amidah, and Birkat HaMazon, the grace after meals you met two days ago. The three pillars of daily prayer. The Talmud explains the Shema in a lovely way. Shema means hear, and some sages read it as: hear in any language that you hear, that you understand. If the words don't reach you, what have you heard? Grace is a blessing, and you can't really thank someone in words you don't follow. The Amidah is a plea for mercy, and you plead in whatever words you have. Not everything is on that list. The Mishnah has a second list of things that must be said in Hebrew, like the priestly blessing. And Hebrew holds a special place: the language of the Torah and the prayer book, shared by Jews far apart. Many authorities in Jewish law say it's best to pray in Hebrew if you understand it, and some say Hebrew should be used even if you don't. Reform prayer books include a great deal of the vernacular; Orthodox prayer books keep the Hebrew and print translations beside it. Communities weigh it differently. But the Mishnah's baseline stands: the Shema, the Amidah and grace are valid in a language you understand. In the Mishnah's view, prayer doesn't wait for the right accent.
screen: `THE SHEMA, THE AMIDAH, THE GRACE.` · `SHEMA: HEAR, IN WHAT YOU HEAR.` · `SOME THINGS STAY IN HEBREW.` · `COMMUNITIES WEIGH IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `ANY LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Use the language you dreamed in as a child, the one your grandmother scolded you in, and say something slowly in it: a short prayer or blessing if you pray, or something you're grateful for, out loud, if you don't, and notice whether it lands differently. If English is your only language, say it in the plainest English you can, the way you'd say it to a child.
Any language. The Mishnah's ruling that the Shema, the Amidah and the grace after meals may be said in any language you understand.
Your line: God understands every language. Hebrew keeps its place, and your own words count too. See you tomorrow.

641.title: Siddur close: prayer shapes the day
641.hook: morning, afternoon, evening, Shabbat, festivals: the prayer book is a map of time
641.tomorrow: Elul: the king in the field
641.howItsDone: Observant Jews pray three services daily, Shacharit, Mincha and Maariv, with added prayers for Shabbat, the new moon and festivals, all laid out in the siddur; many others keep one or two prayers, like Modeh Ani or the Shema at bedtime.

segments.voice: Yesterday, any language: the Shema, the Amidah and the grace, valid in words you understand. Your line was God understands every language. Today, the prayer book closes.

Back on day five hundred thirty-eight, you opened a book. A siddur. The word means order. For a hundred and four days you've walked it, roughly in the order it's prayed. The morning blessings and the rooster. The warm-up psalms. The Shema with a hand over the eyes. The Amidah on your feet. Kaddish, Aleinu, the afternoon pause, the evening's shelter. Shabbat welcomed like a bride. The festivals, the Days of Awe, and this last week, the prayers that live outside the book.
screen: `A BOOK CALLED ORDER.` → `A HUNDRED AND FOUR DAYS.` → `FROM THE ROOSTER TO THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Step back and look at the whole siddur, and it isn't really organized by topic. It's organized by time, a map of the clock and the calendar. Morning, afternoon, evening: three services a day. The Talmud links them to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and Genesis gives Isaac a beautiful moment for the afternoon: "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." A psalm names all three times in a row: "Evening, and morning, and at noonday, will I complain, and moan; and He hath heard my voice." Then the week: six weekdays with their requests, and Shabbat, when the requests go quiet and the Amidah becomes one long breath of holiness. Then the month, with the new moon. Then the year: the festivals with Hallel, the Days of Awe with their own thick book. Then a life: a prayer for a journey, a blessing after food, the Kaddish after a death. Open the siddur anywhere and the first question it answers is: what time is it? That's the deep idea. Prayer in this tradition isn't mainly something you do when you feel like it. It's a rhythm laid over time, so the day itself has a shape. The day wakes into thanks, pauses in the middle, and lies down into shelter. The prayers come back around until the day is held by them, the way a riverbank holds the river. Next comes the year itself, beginning with Elul.
screen: `ORGANIZED BY TIME, NOT TOPIC.` · `MORNING, AFTERNOON, EVENING.` · `THE WEEK, THE MONTH, THE YEAR.` · `WHAT TIME IS IT?` · then, large: `PRAYER SHAPES THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Look back over the whole walk, the morning blessings, the rooster's understanding, the Shema, the Amidah's open my lips, Birkat HaMazon, the evening's spread over us, the traveler's prayer, five words for someone sick, and pick the one that stayed with you. Decide when in your day it would live: morning, midday, a meal, or night. If you pray, say it now, once, slowly; if not, hold it as a line to live by.
Siddur. Order: the prayer book's name, read today as a map of time, day, week, month, year and a life.
Your line: prayer shapes the day. The book closes, and the clock keeps its shape. That's day six hundred forty-one.

642.title: Elul: the king in the field
642.hook: Shneur Zalman's parable: in Elul the king walks out to meet people in the fields
642.carry: the king is in the field
642.howItsDone: During Elul many Jews take stock of the past year, add Psalm 27 to daily prayer, give more charity and prepare for Rosh Hashanah; in Chabad and other Hasidic communities Shneur Zalman's parable of the king in the field is often retold.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the siddur closed. Your line was prayer shapes the day. Today, a new stretch of the path, the Jewish year in depth, starting with the month before the new year.

To see a king in the old world, you had to earn it. You traveled to the capital and waited outside the palace. Guards checked who you were. Officials decided whether you mattered enough. If you got in at all, you bowed, said your piece fast, and were walked out. Now suppose that once a year the king leaves the palace and rides out into the countryside, and anyone working in the fields can walk right up to him.
screen: `TO SEE A KING, YOU EARNED IT.` → `GUARDS, OFFICIALS, WAITING.` → `ONCE A YEAR, HE RIDES OUT.`

segments.voice: This parable comes from Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, the founder of Chabad Hasidism. He told it about Elul, the last month of the Jewish year, just before Rosh Hashanah. Before a king enters his city, he says, the people go out to meet him in the field. There anyone may approach, and he receives them all with a pleasant face, a shining countenance. Farmers in their work clothes, no appointment. Then he enters the city, and they follow him to the palace, where only invited guests get in. The palace is Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: the grand, awesome days, the full congregation, the long services. The field is Elul, the quiet month before, when the closeness is easy and anyone can come as they are. There's an old way of finding Elul in a verse, too. The Song of Songs says: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine." In Hebrew, ani l'dodi v'dodi li. The first letters of those four words, aleph, lamed, vav, lamed, spell Elul, so the month is read as a love song between God and the people. During Elul many communities add Psalm 27 to their daily prayers, a psalm about seeking God's face and hoping to dwell in God's house. The month before judgment could be a month of dread. Shneur Zalman makes it a month of closeness. The king is out in the field, and the field is where you already are.

segments.voice: Step outside if you can, or go to a window, and look at what's actually there: the street, a tree, the sky, a parked car, without dressing it up. This is the field. If you pray, picture the king of the parable out here in the ordinary, receiving you as you are; if not, let yourself meet the day without preparing for it first.

643.title: Elul: getting ready
643.hook: the shofar sounds on Elul mornings, and prayers for forgiveness begin
643.howItsDone: In Ashkenazi synagogues the shofar is blown after weekday morning prayers during Elul, and selichot begin the Saturday night before Rosh Hashanah; Sephardi communities recite selichot early each morning throughout Elul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shneur Zalman's parable. Your line was the king is in the field. Today, how the field gets noisy.

A weekday morning in late summer. The service is ending, people are folding their prayer shawls, someone is already checking their phone. Then, from the front, a sound cuts through everything: a ram's horn. A long, raw blast, then broken notes, then a long one again. It isn't a holiday. It's an ordinary Tuesday in Elul, and in many synagogues this happens every weekday morning for a month.
screen: `A WEEKDAY, LATE SUMMER.` → `A RAM'S HORN CUTS THROUGH.` → `EVERY MORNING FOR A MONTH.`

segments.voice: In Ashkenazi communities, the shofar is blown after the morning service through most of Elul, though not on Shabbat and not on the day before Rosh Hashanah. A wake-up call, a month early. The great medieval teacher Maimonides wrote that the shofar seems to say: sleepers, wake up from your sleep; look at your deeds and return. Then come the selichot, the prayers for forgiveness. Selichah means pardon. Sephardi communities rise early and say them through the whole month of Elul. Ashkenazi communities begin later, usually on the Saturday night before Rosh Hashanah, sometimes around midnight, and continue until Yom Kippur. Either way, the heart of every selichot service is the same: the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy. They come from the moment after the golden calf, when God passes before Moses and proclaims: "The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth." The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 17b, pictures God wrapped in a prayer shawl like a prayer leader, showing Moses this order of prayer and promising that whenever Israel recites it, they will be answered. So the selichot repeat it again and again. Why a whole month? Tradition says Moses went back up the mountain for a second set of tablets at the start of Elul, and came down forty days later, on what became Yom Kippur. Elul is the runway: you don't arrive at the Days of Awe cold.
screen: `THE SHOFAR, EVERY WEEKDAY MORNING.` · `SLEEPERS, WAKE UP.` · `SELICHOT: PRAYERS FOR PARDON.` · `THE THIRTEEN ATTRIBUTES.` · then, large: `THIRTY DAYS TO GET READY.`

segments.voice: If you can, play a recording of a shofar, or let the bell at the start of this sit be your wake-up call. When the sound fades, ask one honest question, what from this past year needs looking at, and let it stand without solving it. If you pray, you can say the line from Exodus: merciful and gracious.
Selichot. Prayers for pardon, built around the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, said in the weeks before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
Your line: thirty days to get ready. Sleepers, wake up, and look at your deeds. See you tomorrow.

644.title: Rosh Hashanah: the world's birthday
644.hook: the new year marks the sixth day of creation, when people were made
644.howItsDone: Rosh Hashanah is observed on the first two days of Tishrei with long synagogue services, the shofar, festive meals with apples and honey and round challah, and the words 'today the world was born' after the shofar in Musaf.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shofar on Elul mornings and the selichot. Your line was thirty days to get ready. Today, the runway ends and the new year begins.

Most new year's celebrations are about a calendar turning over: a countdown, a ball dropping, a kiss at midnight. The Jewish new year sounds different in its prayers. Right after the shofar is blown in the additional service, the congregation says a line in Hebrew: hayom harat olam. Today the world was conceived. Or born. Not a calendar flipping. A birthday. And not the Jewish people's birthday. Everyone's.

Rosh Hashanah means head of the year. Oddly, the Torah never uses that name. It calls the day the first of the seventh month, "a memorial proclaimed with the blast of horns, a holy convocation." The rabbis gave it its famous name. In the Talmud, two great sages argue about when the world was created. Rabbi Eliezer says in the month of Tishrei, in the autumn. Rabbi Yehoshua says Nisan, in the spring. The prayer book follows Rabbi Eliezer for this day: the new year is the world's anniversary. A midrash gets even more precise. If creation began on the twenty-fifth of Elul, then the first of Tishrei, Rosh Hashanah, is the sixth day, the day human beings were made. It tells the first day of Adam's life hour by hour: created, given the breath of life, placed in the garden, given a command, broke it, judged, and pardoned, all before sunset. And God says to him: this is a sign for your children. As you stood before Me in judgment today and went out pardoned, so will they, every year on this day. So Rosh Hashanah holds two things at once: a day of judgment, solemn and serious, and a birthday party for the whole human race. Judgment, in this telling, happens to beloved creatures, on the day they were made.
screen: `HEAD OF THE YEAR.` · `TISHREI OR NISAN?` · `THE SIXTH DAY: PEOPLE ARE MADE.` · `JUDGED AND PARDONED BY SUNSET.` · then, large: `HAPPY BIRTHDAY, WORLD.`

segments.voice: Picture the whole earth, not an idea of it but the actual oceans, a city at night, a crowded train, a baby being born somewhere right now, every one of them sharing this birthday. If you pray, thank God for making the world and the people in it; if not, simply say it, quietly or out loud: happy birthday, world. Let it be as silly and as serious as it is.
Rosh Hashanah. Head of the year. The Jewish new year, remembered as the birthday of the world and the day people were made.

Your line: happy birthday, world. A week of four thanks after eating, let us bless, every language, prayer shaping the day, the king in the field, thirty days to get ready. Day six hundred forty-four, done.
